*Working paper, version 0.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.7 [@CFPB17]. Version 0.2 (May 2026) and earlier versions carried an error in the fuel-switching elasticity; @sec-tecp and Appendix B correct it.*

*Keywords:* carbon pricing; effective carbon price; carbon price equivalent; non-price instruments; energy demand; policy crediting. *JEL:* H23, Q41, Q48, Q54, Q58, C43.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Headline carbon prices misstate how hard countries are pushing on emissions. No country prices carbon with one instrument. A typical package combines a carbon tax or emissions trading in power and industry, fuel excises, renewable subsidies, a clean-fuel standard and efficiency rules. The metrics used to compare countries, the OECD's effective carbon rate and the World Bank's total carbon price, add up explicit and indirect prices per tonne of CO₂ and weight them by emissions [@OECD2023ECR; @Agnolucci2024]. They measure the price signal, not what it achieves. A clean-fuel standard or a renewable subsidy scores nothing, a revenue-neutral feebate scores nothing because its average payment is zero, and a dollar per tonne on coal counts the same as a dollar on gasoline although it cuts far more. The authors of the World Bank measure say so: it describes the incentive, not the mitigation, and an effectiveness-weighted version is future work [@Agnolucci2024, sec. 6.4].

The question this paper answers is what single carbon tax a package of instruments is worth. The Total Effective Carbon Price (TECP) is the uniform economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as the actual policy mix, against the same baseline and over the same horizon. A tax at \$X per tonne on every fuel returns exactly \$X. Any other instrument, price-based or not, is scored by its emission effect in units of that tax.

The concept is not new; a computable, decomposable version is. The IMF defines an economy-wide carbon price equivalent as the carbon price that yields the same emissions reduction as a policy, and computes it for the G20 by re-simulating its Climate Policy Assessment Tool [@black2022framework]. Its proposal for an international carbon price floor would weight fuel taxes by their relative effectiveness at cutting economy-wide emissions [@ParryBlackRoaf2021]. Both need a model run for each policy. This paper derives the metric in closed form from a nested constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) model of energy demand. Abatement weights, computed once per country from the energy balance, delivered prices and two elasticities per sector, convert any package into one number by a weighted sum, and the number splits by sector, by instrument and by margin: fuel switching versus using less energy.

The paper makes five contributions.

1. **The corrected first-order formula** (@sec-tecp). Proposition 1 derives the semi-elasticities from the CES cost function: the switching semi-elasticity is $\sigma_s(e_f/p_{fs} - \kappa_s)$ and the demand semi-elasticity $|\eta_s|\kappa_s$, where $\kappa_s$ is the sector's emissions per dollar of energy spending. The abatement weight of a sector equals its energy spending times $\sigma_s$ times the variance of carbon per dollar across its fuels, plus $|\eta_s|\kappa_s^2$. Proposition 2 shows that the switching margin then moves along the isoquant, so it conserves energy service, as it must. Version 0.2 and all earlier versions carried an extra factor $(1 - w_{fs})$ that breaks this property, and the appendix of version 0.2 counted the term $(e_f - \bar e_s)$ twice, which made the metric depend on the unit of energy.
2. **Accuracy beyond first order** (@sec-exact). The exact TECP is unique (Proposition 3), and a closed-form second-order correction recovers most of the gap between the linear and the full-model value: in the worked example the first-order TECP is 10 percent low, the second-order 1.7 percent.
3. **Non-price instruments** (@sec-nonprice). A tradable standard is a feebate at its credit price (Proposition 4). A non-tradable standard with heterogeneous compliance costs is scored by a responsiveness-weighted average of marginal compliance costs, which reduces to the emission-weighted average when firms respond alike (Proposition 5). Mandates, procurement rules and legal obligations are scored by backing out the price from a modeled emission effect, under stated identification assumptions.
4. **Calibration and uncertainty** (@sec-calibration). Elasticities come from meta-analyses, each cited only for what it estimates, and the uncertainty is carried through to a band by Monte Carlo.
5. **Comparison** (@sec-literature, @sec-example). One stylized economy is scored by the explicit-price metrics, an average-cost implicit price, the IMF's equivalence approach and the TECP. The explicit-price metric says \$21; the TECP says \$33 to first order and \$37 exactly; counting the fuel standard's credit price as a carbon price says \$72.

The metric serves the series it belongs to. Paper 1.1 proposes paying countries per tonne cut by a policy rather than by a project, which needs a common unit for taxes, feebates and standards [@StrettonWP11]. Paper 1.3 proposes that the EU's border mechanism recognize a sector's price signal rather than only the price paid, which needs a measure of that signal for non-price instruments [@StrettonWP13]. @sec-uses sets out both uses and a third, country diagnostics. @sec-limits states what the metric does not measure.

# Related literature and existing metrics {#sec-literature}

Four families of metrics put climate policies on one scale, and only one measures emission effects. Appendix A reviews the literature in full; @tbl-metrics summarizes the comparison and scores the worked example of @sec-example under each.

**Price-signal metrics add explicit and indirect prices and weight them by emissions.** The OECD's effective carbon rate sums carbon taxes, emissions trading prices and fuel excise taxes per tonne of CO₂ for each fuel and sector, and its net version deducts fossil-fuel subsidies [@OECD2023ECR]. The World Bank's total carbon price adds direct pricing to indirect pricing through excises and consumption subsidies, measured by a price-gap method, for 142 countries from 1991 to 2021, so it can turn negative; indirect pricing is most of the global total [@Agnolucci2024]. Both share the TECP's cell structure, fuel by sector, which makes the TECP easy to explain: it keeps the cells' prices and replaces emission weights with abatement weights. Neither counts standards, mandates or subsidies to clean energy. The World Carbon Pricing Database documents explicit instruments by sector [@dolphin2022wcpd]. An econometric estimate on a large cross-country panel finds that a €10 rise in the effective carbon rate cuts fossil CO₂ by 3.7 percent in the long run [@darcangelo2022], a semi-elasticity of the same order as the 0.6 percent per dollar in this paper's example.

**The IMF measures gaps to efficient prices, which is a different object.** Its subsidy estimates compare retail fuel prices with an efficient price that includes supply costs, environmental costs and forgone consumption taxes; explicit subsidies are undercharging for supply costs and implicit subsidies are undercharging for the rest [@ParryBlackVernon2021; @black2023subsidies]. A large implicit subsidy means prices are far from efficient. It does not say how much current policy cuts emissions, and only the explicit part is a policy price that could enter the TECP's cells.

**Implicit carbon prices have meant average cost per tonne.** The OECD's 2013 effective carbon prices divide the cost of each policy by the tonnes it abates, across taxes, trading, feed-in tariffs, capital subsidies and regulations [@oecd2013ecp]. @MarcantoniniEllerman2015 compute the implicit carbon price of German feed-in tariffs this way, at about €57 per tonne for wind and €552 for solar in 2006–2010 (figures from the working-paper version). @AldyPizer2016 note that such prices measure average cost, are model-derived and are high both for costly policies and for those that abate little. A metric of this kind ranks an expensive policy as ambitious. The TECP ranks it by what it cuts. "Implicit carbon price" has also meant the shadow cost of a regulation and indirect pricing through fuel taxes [@Agnolucci2024, n. 1]; @Carhart2022 extend comprehensive carbon prices to portfolio standards, feed-in tariffs and fuel standards.

**Carbon price equivalents measure emission effects, and the TECP is one.** @black2022framework define the economy-wide and sectoral carbon price equivalents as the price that yields the same CO₂ cut as a policy, computed by simulating the policy in CPAT and searching for the matching carbon price. For the G20 in 2030 they find equivalents above \$150 per tonne for some power-sector renewables and coal phase-out targets, and \$5–40 per tonne from existing fuel taxes. CPAT represents non-price policies by shadow prices on the efficiency margin [@black2023cpat]. The IMF's price-floor proposal accepts "emissions-equivalent alternatives to carbon pricing" and proposes weighting fuel taxes by relative effectiveness [@ParryBlackRoaf2021], and the 2019 Fiscal Monitor reportedly gives first-pass effective carbon prices that account for differences in responsiveness [@ParryBlackRoaf2021, n. 26; @IMF2019FM]. The exact TECP of @sec-exact is the same object as the economy-wide equivalent. The differences are in construction and use: a closed-form linear version that needs no model run, weights that belong to the economy and can be published, a split by margin that explains why feebates, standards and portfolio standards deliver less abatement per dollar of shadow price than a tax, an explicit theory of non-price instruments, and an uncertainty band.

| Metric | What it counts | How it aggregates | Non-price instruments | What it misses | Example mix (\$/t) |
|---|---|---|---|---|--:|
| Effective carbon rate (OECD) | Carbon taxes, trading prices, fuel excises; net version less fossil-fuel subsidies | Emission-weighted average | Not counted | Responsiveness; standards; clean-energy subsidies | 20.8 |
| Total carbon price (World Bank) | Direct pricing plus excises net of consumption subsidies (price gap) | Emission-weighted average | Not counted | As above | 20.8 |
| Price gap to efficient prices (IMF) | Gap between retail and efficient fuel prices | Dollars of subsidy by fuel | Not counted | Not a policy price; says nothing about emission effects | n.a. |
| Average-cost implicit price (OECD 2013 type) | Cost of a policy per tonne abated | Per instrument | Counted at average cost | Marginal effect; ranks costly policies high | 78.5 (subsidy) |
| Shadow prices counted as prices | Explicit prices plus credit prices of standards | Covered-emission-weighted | Counted at shadow price | Size and responsiveness of the base | 71.8 |
| Carbon price equivalent (IMF) | Uniform price with the same emission cut, by model re-simulation | Model | Shadow prices in CPAT | Needs a model run per policy; no closed-form weights | 36.9 |
| TECP (this paper) | Uniform tax with the same emission cut | Abatement-weighted average of price wedges; exact by iteration | Credit price, weighted compliance cost or backed-out effect | Cost and welfare; leakage outside the model | 33.2 (first order); 36.9 (exact); 32.4–38.1 (range) |

The economy has no fuel excises or fossil-fuel subsidies, so the two price-signal metrics coincide; the average-cost price is the subsidy's budgetary cost per tonne avoided; "shadow prices counted as prices" adds the fuel standard's \$166 credit price on road-fuel emissions; the IMF equivalent is computed here in the same model as the exact TECP, so the two coincide by construction. Range: 5th–95th percentile across calibrations (@sec-calibration). Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`. {#tbl-metrics}

**The emission-effect literature on individual instruments supplies the decomposition's logic.** @FischerNewell2008 decompose each power-sector instrument into implicit taxes and subsidies by technology and rank them by cost for a given cut: an emissions price, then a performance standard, a fossil output tax, a renewable portfolio standard, a renewable subsidy and research subsidies. A portfolio standard is a small tax on fossil output and a larger subsidy to renewables, with no conservation incentive. @HollandHughesKnittel2009 show that a low-carbon fuel standard taxes high-carbon fuel and subsidizes low-carbon fuel and cannot be efficient; @goulder2016 find that a clean energy standard leans on fuel switching and gets much less demand reduction than cap-and-trade. In the TECP these are statements about the demand margin: such instruments have small or negative extensive carbon prices, so their TECP lies well below their shadow price.

**The model is standard; its use for a policy metric is not.** The nested CES goes back to @Sato1967, and the elasticity matrix it implies, two parameters per sector plus observed cost shares, is the backbone of energy demand in CPAT [@black2023cpat]. CPAT splits elasticities into a usage margin and an efficiency margin; the TECP splits them into fuel switching and conservation, a different axis that maps onto the price wedges instruments create.

# Energy demand: nested CES with partial adjustment {#sec-model}

**Each sector minimizes the cost of an energy service produced from several fuels, and buys less service when it costs more.** The economy has sectors $s$ (power, transport, industry, buildings) and fuels $f$. Sector $s$ uses $q_{fs}$ units of fuel $f$ at delivered price $p_{fs}$, which includes existing taxes. Fuel $f$ emits $e_f$ tonnes of CO₂ per unit, so baseline emissions are $E_{fs} = e_f q_{fs}$ and $E_s = \sum_f E_{fs}$. Fuels combine into a service $Q_s$ through a CES aggregator with elasticity of substitution $\sigma_s$:
$$
Q_s = \Big[\sum_f \alpha_{fs}^{1/\sigma_s}\, q_{fs}^{(\sigma_s-1)/\sigma_s}\Big]^{\sigma_s/(\sigma_s-1)},
$$ {#eq-ces}
with unit cost $C_s(p) = \big(\sum_f \alpha_{fs}\, p_{fs}^{1-\sigma_s}\big)^{1/(1-\sigma_s)}$. Demand for the service has constant price elasticity $-\eta_s$, with $\eta_s \ge 0$ written as a positive number throughout: $Q_s = \bar Q_s\, (C_s/\bar C_s)^{-\eta_s}$. Cost minimization gives fuel demand $q_{fs} = Q_s\, \alpha_{fs}\, (p_{fs}/C_s)^{-\sigma_s}$. The share parameters $\alpha_{fs}$ are calibrated so that the baseline reproduces observed quantities.

**Three statistics of the baseline summarize each sector.** Energy spending is $X_s = \sum_f p_{fs} q_{fs}$ and fuel $f$'s cost share $s_{fs} = p_{fs}q_{fs}/X_s$. Carbon per dollar of fuel $f$ is $x_{fs} = e_f/p_{fs}$. The sector's carbon per dollar of energy spending is the cost-share-weighted mean,
$$
\kappa_s = \sum_f s_{fs}\, x_{fs} = E_s / X_s ,
$$ {#eq-kappa}
and the dispersion of carbon per dollar across fuels is $V_s = \sum_f s_{fs}(x_{fs} - \kappa_s)^2$. A sector with one fuel, or with fuels that emit the same per dollar, has $V_s = 0$: no carbon price can move it by switching. In the worked example, power emits 8.2 kg of CO₂ per dollar of energy spending, industry 7.9 kg and road transport 2.3 kg, because motor fuel is expensive per unit of carbon.

**A policy that changes delivered prices moves quantities through a known formula.** Let a policy change prices by $\Delta p_{fs}$, write $\pi_{fs} = \Delta p_{fs}/p_{fs}$ for the proportional change and $P_{fs} = 1 + \pi_{fs}$. Relative to the baseline, the CES gives exactly
$$
\frac{q'_{fs}}{q_{fs}} = P_{fs}^{-\sigma_s}\,\Big(\frac{C'_s}{C_s}\Big)^{\sigma_s - \eta_s}, \qquad
\frac{C'_s}{C_s} = \Big(\sum_f s_{fs}\, P_{fs}^{1-\sigma_s}\Big)^{1/(1-\sigma_s)} .
$$ {#eq-exact}
Only observed cost shares and the two elasticities enter: the share parameters drop out. To first order, with $\bar\pi_s = \sum_f s_{fs}\pi_{fs}$ the change in the sector's cost index,
$$
d\ln q_{fs} = \underbrace{-\sigma_s\,(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s)}_{\text{fuel switching}} \;\underbrace{-\;\eta_s\,\bar\pi_s}_{\text{demand}} .
$$ {#eq-firstorder}
The first term reallocates use among fuels in proportion to how far each fuel's price moves relative to the sector's cost index. The second scales all fuels down with the cost index. This is the isoelastic form of the CES: the elasticity of fuel $f$ with respect to the price of fuel $g$ is $\varepsilon_{fg} = -\sigma_s\delta_{fg} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{gs}$, an $n \times n$ matrix generated by two parameters and the cost shares, with symmetry and the adding-up conditions built in (Appendix C).

**The CES discipline matters because unconstrained elasticities do not add up.** An isoelastic model with free own- and cross-price elasticities needs $n^2$ parameters per sector and, estimated piecemeal, rarely satisfies the restrictions that make switching conserve energy service. The cost of the discipline is that one $\sigma_s$ governs every pair of fuels in a sector. Stern's meta-analysis finds pair-specific substitution elasticities in industry ranging from about 0.4 for coal–electricity to about 2.1 for coal–gas [@Stern2012], so a single $\sigma_s$ is an average. Where the spread matters, a further nest, gas and coal within fossil fuels and fossil against clean, removes most of it.

**Fuel switching needs new capital; using less energy does not, so the two margins adjust at different speeds.** Write fuel demand as $q_{fs} = Q_s\, h_{fs}(p)$, where $h_{fs}$ is the unit input requirement of fuel $f$ per unit of service; the switching term of @eq-firstorder moves $\ln h_{fs}$ and the demand term moves $\ln Q_s$. Each moves a fixed fraction of the way to its new equilibrium each year:
$$
\ln h_{fs,t} = \ln h_{fs,t-1} + \lambda^{I}_s\big(\ln h^{*}_{fs,t} - \ln h_{fs,t-1}\big), \qquad
\ln Q_{s,t} = \ln Q_{s,t-1} + \lambda^{X}_s\big(\ln Q^{*}_{s,t} - \ln Q_{s,t-1}\big).
$$ {#eq-adjust}
After a permanent price change, the switching margin has completed a fraction $a^I_s(T) = 1 - (1-\lambda^I_s)^T$ of its long-run response by year $T$, and the demand margin $a^X_s(T) = 1 - (1-\lambda^X_s)^T$. The horizon-$T$ elasticities are $a^I_s(T)\sigma_s$ and $a^X_s(T)\eta_s$, and with one-year and long-run estimates from the literature, $\lambda \approx \varepsilon^{SR}/\varepsilon^{LR}$ [@Labandeira2017; @havranek2012]. Switching between fuels in vehicles, boilers and furnaces follows capital turnover, a few percent of the stock a year [@black2022framework, Annex C, for vehicles]; behavioral demand responds within one or two years. So $\lambda^I_s$ is small and $\lambda^X_s$ large. Version 0.2 attached the fast speed to the switching margin and described it as conservation; that labeling is corrected here (Appendix C). Splitting the adjustment into the two CES components, rather than into energy shares and total energy as in version 0.2, keeps the switching margin on the isoquant at every date.

**Technical efficiency changes units, not the TECP.** Version 0.2 expressed prices and emission factors per unit of useful energy, $p/\varphi$ and $e/\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is conversion efficiency. Carbon per dollar, $x = e/p$, and cost shares are unchanged by that rescaling, so every result below holds whether quantities are measured in final or useful energy. Efficiency matters only where Proposition 2(ii) refers to equal prices per unit of service.

# The Total Effective Carbon Price {#sec-tecp}

**The TECP is defined by an emission cut, not by a formula.** Let $R(\tau)$ be the full-model emission cut, relative to the baseline and at horizon $T$, from a carbon tax of $\tau$ per tonne on every fuel in every sector, so that $\Delta p_{fs} = \tau e_f$. Let $R_P$ be the cut from a policy mix $P$, in the same model, against the same baseline and at the same horizon.

**Definition 1 (TECP).** *The Total Effective Carbon Price of $P$ is the $\tau^*$ that solves $R(\tau^*) = R_P$.*

The definition says what the TECP measures: abatement, in units of a uniform tax. Proposition 3 below shows that $\tau^*$ exists and is unique. Computing it needs the full model; the first-order version needs only weights.

**To first order, the TECP is a weighted average of the prices a policy puts on each fuel.** Define the policy's *extensive carbon price* in sector $s$ and its *intensive carbon price* on fuel $f$ as
$$
\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = \frac{\bar\pi_s}{\kappa_s}, \qquad
\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \frac{\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s}{x_{fs} - \kappa_s}.
$$ {#eq-taus}
The extensive price is the uniform carbon tax that would raise the sector's cost index as much as the policy does. The intensive price is the uniform carbon tax that would move fuel $f$'s price relative to the cost index as much as the policy does. Both are in dollars per tonne, and a carbon tax at rate $\tau$ sets both equal to $\tau$ for every fuel in every sector it covers. This normalization fixes the inconsistency between version 0.2, whose main text measured the intensive price in dollars per unit of energy, and the September 2026 variant, which normalized it per tonne; the per-tonne normalization is used throughout. The intensive price is undefined for a fuel whose carbon per dollar equals the sector average, but its product with the semi-elasticity below is always defined.

**Proposition 1 (first-order TECP).** *Let the economy follow the nested CES of @eq-ces, and let a policy change delivered prices by $\Delta p_{fs}$. To first order in the price changes:*

*(i) the emission cut is*
$$
R_P = \sum_s\Big[\sum_f E_{fs}\,\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\,\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} + E_s\,\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_s\,\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s\Big],
\qquad
\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \sigma_s\,(x_{fs} - \kappa_s), \quad
\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_s = \eta_s\,\kappa_s ;
$$ {#eq-cut}
*(ii) a uniform tax of \$1 per tonne cuts emissions by*
$$
\Lambda = \sum_s X_s\big(\sigma_s V_s + \eta_s\kappa_s^2\big) > 0 ;
$$ {#eq-lambda}
*(iii) the first-order TECP is*
$$
\tau^*_{(1)} = \frac{R_P}{\Lambda} = \sum_s\sum_f \Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\,\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} + \sum_s \Omega^{\mathrm{ext}}_s\,\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s,
\qquad
\Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \frac{E_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}}{\Lambda}, \quad
\Omega^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = \frac{E_s\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_s}{\Lambda},
$$ {#eq-tecp}
*with weights that sum to one; and (iv) a uniform tax at rate $\tau$ has $\tau^*_{(1)} = \tau$.*

The proof (Appendix B) differentiates @eq-exact. The semi-elasticities have direct readings. Switching cuts emissions from fuel $f$ in proportion to how far its carbon per dollar exceeds the sector's: a \$1 tax raises fuel $f$'s price by $e_f$, or $x_{fs}$ in proportion, against $\kappa_s$ for the cost index. Demand cuts all of a sector's emissions in proportion to its carbon per dollar of energy spending. A sector's switching weight is $\sigma_s X_s V_s/\Lambda$: large where clean and dirty fuels coexist at very different carbon per dollar and substitute easily. Its demand weight is $\eta_s X_s\kappa_s^2/\Lambda$: large where carbon is a big share of the energy bill. Individual switching weights $\Omega^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}$ are negative for emitting fuels that are cleaner per dollar than their sector's average, such as gas in a coal-heavy power sector, because a carbon tax raises their use; the weights still sum to one across all cells.

**The weights belong to the economy, not the policy.** They depend on the energy balance, delivered prices, emission factors and two elasticities per sector, and they are computed once per country and year. Any package is then evaluated by one weighted sum, transparently and reproducibly, and its TECP splits additively by sector, by margin and by instrument. In the worked example (@fig-weights), power holds 46 percent of emissions but 67 percent of the abatement weight, industry 24 and 27 percent, and road transport 31 percent of emissions but 5.5 percent of the weight, because a dollar per tonne barely moves the price of motor fuel and fuels in transport emit similar amounts per dollar. Fuel switching carries 74 percent of the weight and demand 26 percent.

![Abatement weights and emission shares by sector in the stylized economy. The TECP weights each sector's carbon prices by its share of the abatement from a uniform tax (upper bars), split into the fuel-switching and demand margins; emission-weighted metrics use the share of baseline emissions (lower bars). Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig1_weights.png){#fig-weights width=100%}

**Proposition 2 (the switching margin conserves energy service).** *(i) Under Proposition 1, for any policy, the switching margin leaves each sector's service aggregate unchanged to first order: $\sum_f s_{fs}\,\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\,\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \sigma_s\sum_f s_{fs}(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) = 0$, and for a uniform tax $\sum_f s_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = 0$. (ii) Where fuels in a sector have equal prices per unit of service, the switching margin under a uniform tax conserves physical energy: $\sum_f q_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = 0$. (iii) The semi-elasticity of version 0.2 and earlier, $\sigma_s(1 - w_{fs})(e_f - \bar e_s)/p_{fs}$ with energy shares $w_{fs}$ and $\bar e_s = \sum_f w_{fs}e_f$, violates (i) and (ii). With equal prices $p$, its switching margin changes sector energy by $(\sigma_s Q_s/p)\sum_f w_{fs}^2(e_f - \bar e_s)$ per dollar of tax, which is zero only in special cases, such as equal shares.*

The proof is in Appendix B. The economics is that switching moves along an isoquant: at baseline prices, what a sector saves on the fuels it uses less of it spends on the fuels it uses more of. Any change in the scale of energy use belongs to the demand margin. The old factor $(1 - w_{fs})$ came from applying the own-price elasticity holding total energy fixed, $-\sigma_s(1 - s_{fs})$, to a price change already measured relative to the sector average. That drops the cross-price effects of the other fuels' price changes and leaves part of a scale change inside the switching margin. In the example's power sector, the old form makes a \$1 tax *raise* energy service by 0.13 percent through switching, offsetting four fifths of the 0.16 percent cut from the demand margin. The old form rates the policy mix at \$31.7 rather than \$33.2 to first order.

**Version 0.2's appendix compounded the error by counting $(e_f - \bar e_s)$ twice.** Its Appendix A.7 folded $(e_f - \bar e_s)$ and $\bar e_s$ into the semi-elasticities, and A.9 multiplied them by the same terms again in the normalization $\Lambda$, while its main text measured the intensive price in dollars per unit of energy. The weights then carry $(e_f - \bar e_s)^2$ and $\bar e_s^2$, which have units of tonnes squared. A uniform tax still returns itself, which is why the error went unnoticed, but every other policy's score depends on the unit of energy: the example's mix scores \$30.9 with power in megawatt-hours and \$30.1 with power in gigajoules. The TECP of Proposition 1 does not depend on units (Appendix B, B.6).

**The decomposition by margin explains why instruments with the same shadow price differ.** Write $\Lambda = \Lambda^I + \Lambda^X$ for the switching and demand parts and $\omega = \Lambda^I/\Lambda$. Every TECP splits into a switching part and a demand part, $\tau^* = \omega\,\tau^*_I + (1-\omega)\,\tau^*_X$, where the *switching-margin price* $\tau^*_I = \sum_{f,s}E_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}/\Lambda^I$ and the *demand-margin price* $\tau^*_X$ are the policy's average intensive and extensive prices, weighted by abatement. Computed for one sector, $\tau^*_{I,s}$ is the sector's price signal for cleaner production, the quantity border recognition needs (@sec-uses). A revenue-neutral feebate works almost only on the switching margin, a uniform tax per unit of energy works only on the demand margin, and a renewable subsidy has a negative demand-margin price because it lowers the cost of energy.

**Corollary 1 (feebates and same-product routes).** *A feebate at rate $t$ around benchmark $\bar e_s = \sum_f w_{fs}e_f$ changes prices by $\Delta p_{fs} = t(e_f - \bar e_s)$. Its intensive price is $\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = t - t\,\bar e_s\big(1/p_{fs} - \sum_g s_{gs}/p_{gs}\big)/(x_{fs} - \kappa_s)$. It equals $t$ for every fuel, and the extensive price is zero, if and only if the fuels or routes have equal prices per unit of service, as competing routes making the same product do.*

So the statement that a sector's switching-margin price equals its feebate rate holds where routes make the same product at the same price, such as steel from blast furnaces and electric arc furnaces, and only approximately elsewhere. A feebate across fuels with different prices per unit, such as road fuels, has an intensive price that differs from $t$ fuel by fuel and a small nonzero demand-margin price.

**The TECP can be stated at any horizon.** Because the switching margin adjusts slowly and the demand margin fast, short-run and long-run TECPs weight the margins differently.

**Corollary 2 (horizon TECP).** *Under the partial adjustment of @eq-adjust, the first-order TECP at horizon $T$ is Proposition 1 with $\sigma_s$ and $\eta_s$ replaced by $a^I_s(T)\sigma_s$ and $a^X_s(T)\eta_s$, both in the policy's cut and in the benchmark tax's. With common speeds across sectors,*
$$
\tau^*_T = \omega_T\,\tau^*_I + (1 - \omega_T)\,\tau^*_X, \qquad \omega_T = \frac{a^I(T)\,\omega}{a^I(T)\,\omega + a^X(T)\,(1-\omega)} .
$$ {#eq-horizon}

In the example, the switching margin's long-run share of the weight is 74 percent and, after one year, 36 percent. An instrument that works by switching, such as a feebate, a renewable subsidy or a fuel standard, therefore has a short-run TECP well below its long-run TECP relative to a tax. The long-run TECP says what a maintained package delivers; the short-run TECP says what it delivers before capital turns over. Both compare a policy with a uniform tax that has had the same time to work.

# Beyond first order {#sec-exact}

**The first-order TECP is a ratio of two linear approximations, so its errors partly cancel.** The full CES response is curved: each further dollar of tax cuts less, because the dirtiest fuel's share shrinks. In the example's policy mix, the carbon tax raises the delivered price of coal in industry by 71 percent and of coal power by 41 percent. Linearized, the mix cuts 53 Mt; in the full model, 41 Mt. A linear approximation of a cut that large is poor. But the TECP divides the policy's linear cut by the uniform tax's linear cut, and both overstate in similar proportion. The first-order TECP of the mix, \$33.2, is 10 percent below the exact \$36.9; that of the carbon tax alone, \$28.4, is 4 percent above the exact \$27.2.

**Proposition 3 (exact and second-order TECP).** *(i) The uniform-tax cut $R(\tau)$ is strictly increasing, with $R'(\tau) = \sum_s X_s(\tau)\big[\sigma_s V_s(\tau) + \eta_s\kappa_s(\tau)^2\big]$ evaluated at taxed prices and quantities. So the TECP of Definition 1 exists and is unique for any cut in the range of $R$, which is every cut smaller than baseline emissions when $\eta_s > 0$ in every sector, and it is found by bisection. (ii) To second order in the price changes, the policy's cut is $R_P = R^{(1)}_P + R^{(2)}_P$ with*
$$
R^{(2)}_P = -\sum_s\sum_f E_{fs}\Big\{\tfrac12\big[\sigma_s\pi_{fs}^2 - (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\big(\bar\pi_s^2 + \sigma_s V^\pi_s\big)\big] + \tfrac12 L_{fs}^2\Big\},
$$ {#eq-second}
*where $V^\pi_s = \sum_f s_{fs}(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s)^2$ and $L_{fs} = -\sigma_s\pi_{fs} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\bar\pi_s$, and the second-order TECP is*
$$
\tau^*_{(2)} = \tau^*_{(1)} + \frac{R^{(2)}_P - \tfrac12\,\Gamma\,\big(\tau^*_{(1)}\big)^2}{\Lambda}, \qquad \Gamma = R''(0),
$$ {#eq-tecp2}
*with error of third order. (iii) The first-order TECP is exact to second order if and only if the policy's cut curves as much as that of the uniform tax with the same first-order cut: $R^{(2)}_P = \tfrac12\Gamma(\tau^*_{(1)})^2$.*

Part (iii) says when the linear formula is good enough. For a carbon tax with partial coverage, the policy's curvature resembles the benchmark's and the first-order TECP is close. For a mix that adds a subsidy, whose cut grows faster than linearly as the clean fuel's price falls, the curvatures differ and the first-order TECP understates. Both $R^{(2)}_P$ and $\Gamma$ are closed-form sums over the same cells as $\Lambda$, so the correction costs no more than the first-order formula and should always be reported beside it. In the example $\Gamma$ is negative, $-0.042$ Mt per (\$/t)², the curvature of diminishing returns.

![First-order, second-order and exact TECP in the stylized economy. A: the policy mix of @sec-example scaled by $k$; at $k = 1$ the first-order TECP is \$33.2, the second-order \$36.2 and the exact \$36.9. B: the carbon tax on power and industry alone, at rates up to \$150 per tonne. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig2_accuracy.png){#fig-accuracy width=100%}

**The second-order correction removes most of the error over the range that matters.** @fig-accuracy scales the example's mix and, separately, the carbon tax. For the mix, the first-order error is 5 percent at half the example's instruments, 10 percent at the example and 20 percent at twice it; the second-order error is 0.4, 1.7 and 6 percent. For the tax alone, the first-order TECP overstates by 4 percent at \$30 and 14 percent at \$100; the second-order is within 2 percent up to \$100. The practical rule follows. Use the first-order formula for weights, decompositions and ranking packages. Report the second-order TECP as the headline when its correction exceeds about 5 percent. Use the exact TECP, by bisection on @eq-exact, when the correction exceeds about 10 percent or when the number will settle a payment.

**Exact TECPs do not add across instruments, and the first-order ones do.** In the example the three instruments' stand-alone exact TECPs sum to \$32.7 while the mix's is \$36.9, although the instruments' exact cuts nearly add (41.0 Mt alone against 40.7 Mt together). The gap comes from the benchmark: each further tonne needs a higher uniform tax, so a cut made of several instruments maps to a higher tax than the sum of their separate equivalents. The convention used here is to report the package's exact TECP and to attribute it to instruments by their first-order contributions, which add up and are scaled to the exact total.

# Non-price instruments {#sec-nonprice}

**A binding rule has no rate but has a shadow price, and the TECP needs either that price or the rule's emission effect.** Standards, mandates, procurement rules and legal obligations cut emissions without a per-tonne charge. They enter the TECP by one of two routes. The shadow-price route converts the rule into the price changes it causes and applies Proposition 1 or Definition 1. The back-out route takes the rule's emission effect from a model or an evaluation and finds the uniform tax that delivers the same cut. This section sets out when each route applies and what it assumes.

**Proposition 4 (tradable standards).** *Let a sector face a binding intensity standard $\sum_f e_f q_{fs} \le \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}}\sum_f q_{fs}$, with credits traded competitively at price $\lambda$ per tonne and compliance costs passed through to fuel prices. Then (i) the sector's choices are those of a cost-minimizer facing prices $p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})$: the standard is a feebate at rate $\lambda$ with benchmark $\bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}}$; (ii) its first-order TECP is Proposition 1 with $\Delta p_{fs} = \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})$, and its exact TECP is Definition 1 with $\lambda$ solving the binding constraint in @eq-exact; (iii) the shadow-price route and the back-out route give the same exact TECP; (iv) a renewable portfolio standard requiring a clean share $\theta$, with credits at $\lambda$ per unit of clean output, is the case $\Delta p = \lambda\theta$ on each fossil unit and $-\lambda(1-\theta)$ on each clean unit.*

The proof compares first-order conditions (Appendix B). With competitive trading, each supplier's marginal cost of compliance equals the credit price [@Montgomery1972], so the credit price is the shadow price of the constraint, and the low-carbon fuel standard's implicit tax on high-carbon fuel and subsidy to low-carbon fuel [@HollandHughesKnittel2009] is exactly a feebate. Part (iv) reproduces @FischerNewell2008's decomposition of a portfolio standard into a small fossil output tax and a larger renewable subsidy. Because it charges every fossil unit the same, it does not separate coal from gas, and the TECP shows the cost of that in a low switching-margin price.

*Identification.* The credit price measures the shadow price under four conditions. The market is competitive and clears; if a price ceiling or compliance payment binds, the ceiling is the shadow price. Banking and borrowing allow intertemporal arbitrage, so the price reflects the marginal cost of the path, not only the current year. Pass-through to delivered prices is complete, or its rate is known. The standard's coverage is known, so the price is applied only to covered fuels. A standard that does not bind has a credit price of zero and a TECP of zero, which is the right answer.

**Proposition 5 (non-tradable standards).** *Let firms $i = 1, \dots, m$ in a sector each face their own binding standard, with shadow price $\mu_i$ per tonne, the marginal cost of compliance. Let $E_i$ be firm $i$'s emissions and $r_i$ its first-order cut per tonne of its emissions per \$1 of a feebate at its own benchmark, and write $\Lambda^F = \sum_i E_i r_i$. Then to first order (i) the standard's TECP is*
$$
\tau^* = \frac{\sum_i E_i\, r_i\, \mu_i}{\Lambda} = \frac{\Lambda^F}{\Lambda}\Big[\bar\mu_E + \frac{\mathrm{Cov}_E(r, \mu)}{\bar r}\Big],
$$ {#eq-nontradable}
*where $\bar\mu_E$ is the emission-weighted mean shadow price, $\bar r$ the emission-weighted mean responsiveness and $\mathrm{Cov}_E$ the emission-weighted covariance; (ii) if firms are equally responsive per tonne, the TECP is the emission-weighted average marginal compliance cost scaled by $\Lambda^F/\Lambda$, the sector feebate's abatement per dollar relative to a uniform tax's; (iii) a tradable standard that achieves the same cut has the same TECP and a lower resource cost.*

Each firm under its own standard behaves as if it faced a feebate at its own shadow price, so the sector's cut is the sum of firm-level feebate responses (Appendix B). The covariance term matters. A regulator that reports the simple average compliance cost overstates the TECP if the firms with the highest marginal costs are also the least responsive, which is common: high marginal costs often mean few options. As an illustration, with equal emissions, shadow prices of \$100 and \$300 per tonne and the high-cost firm half as responsive, the responsiveness-weighted mean is \$167, not \$200. Part (iii) is a reminder that the TECP measures abatement: a regulator that imposes a cut at needlessly high cost gets no credit for the cost.

*Identification.* Proposition 5 needs firm-level marginal compliance costs, usually from the regulator's impact assessment, and firm-level responsiveness, which the CES gives from each firm's fuel mix and prices. Engineering estimates of compliance costs often report averages; the proposition needs marginal costs. Where only a sector-wide average cost per tonne is available, the back-out route is safer.

**Mandates, procurement rules and legal obligations are scored by the emission effect they cause.** Many rules change technology choices directly, with no price to observe: a mandate to retire coal plants, a rule that public works use low-carbon cement, building codes, or the forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers in the consumption track of paper 1.1 [@StrettonWP11]. For these the TECP is backed out: $\tau^* = R^{-1}(\Delta E_P)$ exactly, or $\Delta E_P/\Lambda$ to first order, where $\Delta E_P$ is the rule's effect on emissions.

*Identification.* The backed-out TECP is only as good as $\Delta E_P$, which must satisfy four assumptions. (A1) *Common baseline and horizon*: $\Delta E_P$ is measured against the counterfactual used for $R(\tau)$, with all other instruments in place, at the same horizon. (A2) *Net effect*: $\Delta E_P$ is net of rebound and of leakage within and outside the regulated market. State limits on emissions per mile of new cars in the United States raised emissions in other states and from used cars, offsetting 70–80 percent of the reductions in adopting states [@GoulderJacobsenvanBenthem2012]. (A3) *Consistent behavior*: if $\Delta E_P$ comes from a model, its demand responses must agree with the $\sigma_s$ and $\eta_s$ behind $R(\tau)$; otherwise the TECP compares two models, not two policies. (A4) *Causal attribution*: an ex post evaluation must identify the rule's effect against a counterfactual, not before-and-after emissions.

**Under a binding cap, an overlapping instrument's TECP is zero, and the cap's TECP is the whole effect.** If an emissions trading system caps a sector's emissions and the cap binds, a renewable subsidy or standard inside the capped sector lowers the permit price but not emissions. The rule is then scored at zero, and the cap is scored by backing out the cut from the cap against the baseline, or to first order through the permit price, which is the cap's shadow price. A package of a cap and complementary rules has the TECP of the cap. This is the waterbed effect, and the metric handles it only if the user applies (A1) with the cap in place.

# Calibration and uncertainty {#sec-calibration}

**Two elasticities per sector drive the weights, and the literature pins them down only to ranges.** @tbl-calibration gives the long-run ranges used here, the central values of the worked example and the sources, each cited only for what it estimates. Appendix A, Table A1, gives the evidence by sector and fuel.

| Parameter | Power | Road transport | Industry | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma_s$, long run: range (central) | 1.5–3.0 (2.0) | 0.5–1.5 (1.5) | 0.5–1.5 (0.8) | Clean versus dirty inputs: above 1 [@papageorgiou2017]. Among fossil fuels, sector estimates below 1, lowest in power and transport [@serletis2010ej]. Industry, by fuel pair: about 0.4–2.1 [@Stern2012] |
| $\eta_s$, long run: range (central) | 0.2–0.5 (0.2) | 0.3–0.8 (0.4) | 0.3–0.7 (0.3) | Own-price demand elasticities, long-run means: electricity 0.37–0.51, gasoline 0.53–0.77, diesel 0.44, industry 0.51 [@Labandeira2017, via @cpat2022technotes]; gasoline after correcting for publication bias 0.31 [@havranek2012] |
| $\lambda^X$, demand adjustment per year | 0.25–0.40 (0.35) | same | same | Ratio of short- to long-run demand elasticities: gasoline about 0.29 after bias correction [@havranek2012]; about 0.3–0.4 from meta-analytic means [@Labandeira2017] |
| $\lambda^I$, switching adjustment per year | 0.04–0.10 (0.07) | same | same | Capital turnover: vehicles about 6.7 percent a year in CPAT [@black2022framework, Annex C]; boilers, furnaces and plants slower |

: Calibration of the nested CES: long-run substitution and demand elasticities and adjustment speeds. Central values are those of the worked example, which follows the brief; Monte Carlo draws are uniform on each range, independently. Elasticities are written as positive numbers. The short-run means from @Labandeira2017 are taken second-hand and are marked for checking in the bibliography. {#tbl-calibration}

**Each source supports one column, and the old calibration cited them for more.** Version 0.2 cited @Stern2012 and @Labandeira2017 for substitution elasticities in all sectors. Stern's meta-analysis covers interfuel substitution in industry, manufacturing and the whole economy, not power, transport or buildings. Labandeira and coauthors estimate own-price demand elasticities, not substitution elasticities. Sector-level evidence on substitution among fossil fuels finds elasticities below one in every sector, lowest in power generation and transport [@serletis2010ej]. A power-sector $\sigma$ of 2 or more is defensible only for substitution between clean and dirty generation, where nested-CES estimates exceed one [@papageorgiou2017], and that is the nest the example's power sector represents: coal and gas against renewables. Calibration must also respect the CES structure. A fuel's total own-price elasticity is $-\sigma_s + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{fs}$, so an estimate for one fuel identifies $\sigma_s$ and $\eta_s$ only jointly with the cost shares; for a dominant fuel it is close to $-\eta_s$, for a minor fuel close to $-\sigma_s$.

**The example's central values sit at the edges of some ranges.** The demand elasticities for power and industry, 0.2 and 0.3, are at the bottom of the meta-analytic ranges, and the transport substitution elasticity, 1.5, is at the top of a range resting on weak evidence. The central case is kept for consistency with the brief; the Monte Carlo draws span the ranges.

**Meta-analytic elasticities are biased upward in magnitude, and the bias matters most for demand.** Correcting for selective reporting, @havranek2012 find that the mean price elasticity of gasoline demand falls from about −0.23 to −0.09 in the short run and from −0.69 to −0.31 in the long run, roughly halving both. Since demand semi-elasticities enter $\Lambda$ and the instruments' cuts alike, a uniform bias cancels from the TECP; a bias that differs by sector shifts weight toward the sectors whose elasticities are least overstated. The demand ranges in @tbl-calibration run from the bias-corrected values to the uncorrected means.

![Uncertainty in the TECP of the stylized economy: 2,000 draws of the elasticities from the ranges in @tbl-calibration. A: the exact TECP of the policy mix in the long run and after one year (adjustment speeds also drawn); the explicit-price metric is \$20.8 in every draw. B: 5th–95th percentile and median of each instrument's stand-alone exact TECP (blue: long run; orange: one year). The fuel standard enters through its credit price, re-solved in each draw. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig3_uncertainty.png){#fig-uncertainty width=100%}

**Carried through the model, the elasticity uncertainty gives a band of \$32–38 per tonne for the example's mix in the long run.** @fig-uncertainty shows 2,000 draws. The long-run exact TECP of the mix has a median of \$35.3 and a 90 percent range of \$32.4–38.1; the first-order TECP, \$31.3–33.4. After one year the exact TECP is \$24.8–30.7. In every draw, long run or one year, the TECP exceeds the explicit-price metric's \$20.8. The band is narrow relative to the elasticity ranges because the TECP is a ratio: higher elasticities raise both the mix's cut and the benchmark's. What moves it is the relative responsiveness of sectors and margins. The fuel standard's credit price is far more uncertain, \$171–382 per tonne, because a fixed intensity target costs more to meet when substitution is harder; its TECP stays at \$0.7–1.1. The band covers elasticity uncertainty only, not model structure, data errors or the salience question below.

**Taxes may move demand more than equal market price changes, and a price-elasticity calibration then understates explicit taxes.** Several studies find that fuel demand responds more to tax changes than to equal changes in tax-exclusive prices: about three times as much for gasoline taxes in US states, working largely through vehicle choice [@li2014]; a carbon-tax elasticity of gasoline demand three times the price elasticity in Sweden [@andersson2019]; and larger responses in instrumental-variable estimates that exploit tax changes [@davis2011]. If taxes are more salient, the uniform tax that defines the TECP is more effective than a price-calibrated $\Lambda$ says, and non-tax instruments, whose price wedges reach buyers as ordinary price changes, are worth less in units of it. Applying a salience factor of 3 to the demand margin of taxes only, the example's subsidy falls from \$3.7 to \$2.4 and the fuel standard from \$1.2 to \$0.8 at first order, and the mix from \$33.2 to \$30.3. The evidence comes from road fuels, and its persistence and transfer to other sectors are open. A user who adopts it should state the factor and apply it only to the price changes that come from taxes.

# A worked example {#sec-example}

**A stylized economy shows how far the TECP and the existing metrics diverge.** The economy has three sectors with 261 Mt of baseline CO₂ (Appendix D, @tbl-economy): power, with coal, gas and renewables (119 Mt); road transport, with gasoline, diesel and biofuel (80 Mt); and industry, with coal, oil and gas (62 Mt). Delivered prices include existing taxes. Elasticities are the central values of @tbl-calibration. All numbers are stylized, and the economy is the one in the brief [@CFPB17], so the two report the same results.

**The policy mix has a tax, a subsidy and a standard.** A carbon tax of \$30 per tonne covers power and industry. A subsidy of \$10 per MWh goes to renewable generation. A tradable low-carbon fuel standard requires road fuels' carbon intensity per unit of energy to fall 2 percent below its baseline; in the full model it binds at a credit price of \$166 per tonne. A uniform tax of \$1 per tonne on every fuel cuts emissions by 1.59 Mt, 0.61 percent.

| Instrument | Rate or shadow price | Explicit-price metric | Shadow prices counted | TECP, first order: switching + demand | TECP, first order | TECP, exact | Exact, 90% range | Exact, after one year |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Carbon tax, power and industry | \$30/t | 20.8 | 20.8 | 22.0 + 6.4 | 28.4 | 27.2 | 26.0–28.2 | 25.4 |
| Renewable subsidy | \$10/MWh | 0 | 0 | 4.1 − 0.4 | 3.7 | 4.3 | 2.5–4.7 | 1.2 |
| Low-carbon fuel standard, −2% | \$166/t credit price | 0 | 51.1 | 1.0 + 0.2 | 1.2 | 1.2 | 0.7–1.1 | 0.8 |
| **Policy mix** | | **20.8** | **71.8** | **27.1 + 6.1** | **33.2** | **36.9** | **32.4–38.1** | **28.3** |

: The stylized policy mix under four measures, \$ per tonne of CO₂. Explicit-price metric: emission-weighted average explicit carbon price, as in effective-carbon-rate measures. Shadow prices counted: the same with the standard's credit price treated as a carbon price on road-fuel emissions. First-order TECP columns add across instruments; exact TECPs are stand-alone for instruments and for the mix as a whole, so they do not add (@sec-exact). The 90 percent range is from the Monte Carlo of @sec-calibration. After one year: central adjustment speeds, with the standard at its long-run credit price. Second-order TECPs: tax \$27.2, subsidy \$4.2, standard \$1.2, mix \$36.2. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`. {#tbl-example}

**The TECP rates the mix at \$33 per tonne to first order and \$37 exactly; the explicit-price metric says \$21.** @tbl-example sets out the comparison. The tax alone is worth \$27–28, not \$21, because the explicit-price metric divides it over transport's 31 percent of emissions, which hold only 5.5 percent of the abatement weight. The renewable subsidy adds \$3.7 to first order: \$4.1 through switching, less \$0.4 because cheaper power raises demand. The fuel standard binds at \$166 per tonne and adds \$1.2. Counting its credit price as a carbon price, as a naive extension of the effective carbon rate would, puts the mix at \$72: a high price on a large, unresponsive base. The subsidy's budgetary cost per tonne avoided is \$79 (\$514 million on 51 TWh of renewable output for a cut of 6.6 Mt), so an average-cost implicit price would rank it as the most ambitious instrument in the mix; its TECP ranks it a distant second.

**The IMF's equivalence approach and the exact TECP coincide when they use the same model.** Re-simulating the mix and searching for the matching uniform price, as @black2022framework do in CPAT, gives \$36.9 here because the search runs on the same CES. The first-order TECP reaches \$33.2 with one weighted sum and the second-order \$36.2 with two. What the closed form adds is the decomposition: 82 percent of the mix's first-order TECP comes through fuel switching, and almost all of that in power and industry.

**The mix is worth \$28 after one year and \$37 in the long run.** @fig-horizon shows the TECP by horizon under the central adjustment speeds. After one year the subsidy is worth \$1.2, a quarter of its long-run value, because new renewable capacity takes time while the demand response to cheaper power comes quickly. The carbon tax is worth \$25.4 after a year against \$27.2 in the long run, less of a gap because the demand response it triggers is fast. The mix reaches \$33 after ten years. A country that announces this package can claim a long-run TECP of \$37, but in the first years it delivers what a \$28–31 uniform tax would.

![TECP of the stylized mix and its instruments by years since adoption, under partial adjustment with switching speed 0.07 and demand speed 0.35 a year (solid: exact; dotted: first order). Each point compares the policy with a uniform tax that has had the same time to work. The fuel standard is held at its long-run credit price. Source: author's calculation, `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig4_horizon.png){#fig-horizon width=100%}

**The example in the version 0.2 workbook is superseded.** The workbook in `2.Source/` evaluates a \$50 carbon tax, feebates of \$20 in road transport and \$15 in power, and road-fuel excises in two sectors, with renewable generation priced at \$2 per GJ, and reports a TECP of \$61.9. It uses the $(1 - w)$ semi-elasticities that Proposition 2 corrects. Version 0.2's text example, a TECP of "roughly \$75" for a \$50 tax with feebates and excises, was illustrative and not computed. The scripts listed in Appendix D replace both.

# Uses {#sec-uses}

**Policy crediting needs a common unit, and the TECP supplies it.** Paper 1.1 shows that if an outside buyer pays $\pi$ per tonne abated, a feebate at rate $t$ is a net gain for the adopting country whenever $\pi > t/2$, and the country's best response is $t = \pi$ [@StrettonWP11, Prop. 6]. Paying for policies rather than projects requires measuring the tonnes a policy cuts, separately from changes in output and fuel prices. The TECP does this: the tonnes credited for a policy change are $R(\tau^*_{\text{after}}) - R(\tau^*_{\text{before}})$ in the full model, or $\Lambda\,\Delta\tau^*$ to first order. A country that adopts a fuel standard or a procurement rule then earns the same payment per tonne as one that adopts a tax. Because the TECP is a forecast, payments should be settled against observed emissions, and the "change from a benchmark year" design of the IMF price-floor proposal [@ParryBlackRoaf2021] avoids paying for instruments set long ago for other reasons.

**For border recognition, the sector's switching-margin price measures the signal to credit.** The EU's border mechanism reduces an importer's charge by the carbon price "effectively paid" in the country of origin, net of rebates and compensation [@EU2023; @EU2025Omnibus, Art. 9]. A feebate, a rebated tax or an intensity standard pays almost nothing net, so it earns nothing, although its marginal signal is the full rate [@StrettonWP13, Prop. 4]. Paper 1.3 proposes a liability that credits the country-sector price signal alongside the price paid [@StrettonWP13]. The TECP's switching-margin price for the sector, $\tau^*_{I,s}$, is that signal for price and non-price instruments alike: a feebate across routes that make the same product scores its rate (Corollary 1), a tradable standard its credit price (Proposition 4), and a fuel tax or subsidy its per-tonne rate weighted by how strongly the sector's fuel use responds. The demand margin is left out because the border charge is on embodied carbon and the demand response in the importing market comes from the importer's own price. Two cautions apply. Equal emission effects are not equal costs: a regulation at a given shadow price imposes lower private costs on firms than a tax at the same rate, because there is no tax payment on remaining emissions [@keen2022bca; @black2022framework, Annex B]. So recognition on the TECP rewards effort, not competitive burden, and the importer's producers can fairly ask which is being matched. And border credit traditionally rests on average prices paid, while the TECP is a marginal measure [@Agnolucci2024].

**For country diagnostics, the decomposition is the product.** The TECP shows which sectors and margins a package reaches and which it misses. In the example, extending the \$30 tax to road fuels would add only about \$1.6 to the TECP, because transport holds 5.5 percent of the abatement weight. The package's weak point is the low responsiveness of road transport to any carbon price at the margin, which argues for instruments aimed at vehicle choice rather than a higher fuel price. Computed each year from the energy balance, the TECP gives one trajectory for a country's effective carbon price against which announced packages, nationally determined contributions and price-floor commitments can be checked. Published weights also let others reproduce the number, which @AldyPizer2016 identify as a requirement for any metric of comparable effort.

# Limits {#sec-limits}

**The TECP measures abatement, not cost or welfare.** Two packages with the same TECP cut the same tonnes; they need not cost the same. Per tonne, standards and subsidies generally cost more than a price [@FischerNewell2008], static costs per tonne vary widely across instruments [@GillinghamStock2018], and subsidies without carbon pricing can raise mitigation costs several-fold [@KalkuhlEdenhoferLessmann2013]. Replacing a feebate with a tax of equal TECP is not welfare-neutral either: interactions with the existing tax system differ, and a clean energy standard can cost less than cap-and-trade for modest targets because it interacts less with existing taxes [@goulder2016]. The TECP should be reported beside each instrument's shadow price and cost, never instead of them.

**Overlapping instruments do not simply add.** First-order TECPs add by construction, but emission effects interact. Within a binding cap, complementary instruments add nothing (@sec-nonprice). Nested regulations leak, sometimes most of their effect [@GoulderJacobsenvanBenthem2012]. The TECP of a package should come from the package's joint effect, with instrument attribution as a second step.

**The model is partial and static in technology.** It holds incomes, other sectors and the supply of fuels fixed. It does not capture links between sectors, such as the power demand created by electric vehicles, except through the prices the user enters. It credits a solar subsidy only for current abatement, not for the cost declines it may induce [@GillinghamStock2018], and it ignores fossil-fuel supply responses, through which a badly designed subsidy can raise emissions over time [@KalkuhlEdenhoferLessmann2013].

**The inputs inherit the problems of measuring prices.** The intensive and extensive prices come from instrument rates and fuel prices that are hard to measure in many countries. Price-gap estimates confuse market power and distribution costs with taxes, and fuel taxes set for revenue or congestion should not be relabeled as carbon prices [@Agnolucci2024; @ParryBlackRoaf2021]. The TECP improves the weighting, not the measurement of what is weighted.

**Shadow prices can be gamed.** A government that reports its standards' shadow prices has reason to overstate them. Tradable standards have observable credit prices; for non-tradable rules, the back-out route with an independent evaluation is the safer basis, and an independent body could compute TECPs for all countries from a common elasticity set.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

**A policy mix is worth the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions as much, and that number can be computed from an energy balance and two elasticities per sector.** The corrected CES derivation gives switching and demand semi-elasticities whose weights have a simple form: spending times the substitution elasticity times the dispersion of carbon per dollar, plus the demand elasticity times carbon per dollar squared. The switching margin conserves energy service, as the version 0.2 form did not. A second-order correction makes the closed form accurate to within a few percent for packages that raise some fuel prices by more than half, and the exact value follows by bisection. Tradable standards enter at their credit price, non-tradable ones at a responsiveness-weighted average of marginal compliance costs, and mandates through their modeled effect, each under stated assumptions. In a stylized economy the metric rates a mix at \$37 per tonne in the long run, \$32–38 across calibrations and \$28 after one year, where explicit-price metrics say \$21. The main limitation is calibration: elasticities are known to ranges, substitution elasticities outside industry rest on thin evidence, and taxes may be more salient than prices. The next step is to compute the TECP for a G20 country from its energy balance and to compare it with the IMF's model-based equivalent for the same policies.
